title: 1.1 · Every riser in the flight
bodyHtml:
DAY 1 · SESSION 1.1 · CYCLE 1

Every riser in the flight

110-minute long session · B+C double block

TODAY'S LEARNING TARGETS

tr.u2.stair-why. Why the first and last riser are the ones that end up wrong.

Drawing / representation evidence: tr.u2.stair-sect — Draw a stair section with numbered risers and the actual endpoints used.

Success today: Spread 1/8 in. Repeat selected risers with consistent endpoints and an independent checked reference; explain the expected result if setup caused the variation.

THE FIELDHOUSE THREAD TODAY

What students know as today opens: Students can report dimensions, sources and uncertainty limits from Unit 1.

How today connects: Apply the same evidence routine to finished stair surfaces; a pattern is the beginning of diagnosis.

Lesson Flow

Use the 110-minute sequence below. Timings include discussion, transitions and collection.

TimeWhat happens

0–10 min

Diagnostic opening

Teacher: Open the lesson in Present and show its first diagram. Ask: “Different riser readings prove what?” Collect an individual choice and reason before discussion. Reveal: There is observed variation worth checking..

Students produce: A saved opening response; then 60 seconds of partner explanation using the diagram.

Look/listen for: Different risers immediately identify the builder as the cause. Use consistent finished-surface endpoints and repeat with a checked setup. Compare finish changes and measurement setup before diagnosing.

10–25 min

Explain and model

Teacher: State the relationship: Compare vertical rises between finished walking surfaces using consistent endpoints. Variation can come from the stair, floor finishes, setup or reading. Measurements identify a pattern; they do not identify its cause automatically. Model aloud: Provided rises: 7 1/2, 7 9/16, 7 1/2, 7 7/16, 7 1/2 in. Highest - lowest = 7 9/16 - 7 7/16 = 1/8 in. Observed spread is 1/8 in. A compliance decision would also require the applicable stair requirements and measurement confidence. Ask a student to identify the reference, the unit and the evidence supporting the conclusion.

Students produce: An annotated calculation or reference sketch with quantities and units; a prediction before the investigation.

Look/listen for: A reason for each operation. If students repeat the answer without a method, cover the result and have them point to the given quantities.

25–45 min

Investigation and individual record

Teacher: Set up: Rule, level, low stair model or approved observation route. Direct the sequence: 1. Use a low classroom stair model or a facilities-approved accessible stair without obstructing traffic. 2. Number rises from bottom to top; mark consistent finished-surface endpoints. 3. Measure each vertical rise twice; repeat any disagreement with the same setup. 4. Look for a pattern at the ends and compare with possible finish changes. Rotate measurement/checking roles; observe each student rather than inferring skill from a group result.

Students produce: An individual table with quantities, values, units and evidence source. Label supplied data as supplied; keep unexpected results.

Look/listen for: Use consistent finished-surface endpoints and repeat with a checked setup. Compare finish changes and measurement setup before diagnosing.

45–50 min

Stop and check the evidence

Teacher: Pause work, reset tools and compare one example from two students. Ask what was held fixed and whether the recorded values support the claim. Re-model the specific error if needed.

Students produce: A marked correction or a named check to perform next; a brief transition before the second investigation.

Look/listen for: The original result remains visible; a correction includes a reason.

50–70 min

Test an explanation

Teacher: Use this follow-up: Use consistent finished-surface endpoints and repeat with a checked setup. Compare finish changes and measurement setup before diagnosing. Students name one plausible explanation, predict a result and change one relevant factor or compare an independent method. With paper data, test an alternate interpretation of the same stated constraints; do not invent observations.

Students produce: A second evidence record and an explanation of what the comparison supports or leaves unresolved.

Look/listen for: Different risers immediately identify the builder as the cause must be addressed with evidence, not replaced by a new unsupported claim.

70–90 min

Drawing and handoff

Teacher: Assign: Draw a stair section with numbered risers and the actual endpoints used. Partners exchange without an oral explanation first. The reader identifies the datum/endpoints, units and one missing or ambiguous label; the author revises.

Students produce: An individual labelled drawing or setup record, with NTS or a verified scale and a visible revision.

Look/listen for: The representation agrees with the measurements and can be interpreted without the author supplying missing information.

90–103 min

Individual exit and evidence

Teacher: Ask the exact lesson exit: “Using the five supplied rises, state the spread and a test that separates measurement setup from actual riser variation.” Allow the existing frame and word bank; require the same reasoning from every student. Collect before discussing the key.

Students produce: An individual saved exit response or named paper response. Keep observations of actual tool use distinct from supplied-data reasoning.

Look/listen for: Expected response: Spread 1/8 in. Repeat selected risers with consistent endpoints and an independent checked reference; explain the expected result if setup caused the variation.

103–110 min

Feedback, revision and next lesson

Teacher: Return one specific next step. Use the target criteria below; do not turn self-ratings or a correct opening choice into a mastery grade. If the lesson has a self-assessment, complete it after the individual exit. Collect tools and preserve original evidence.

Students produce: A next-check statement and any self-assessment already present in the lesson; teacher notes identify who needs a short recheck.

Look/listen for: A missing response remains not observed, not an invented low score. Begin the next meeting by checking the misconception named below.

IF THE SCHEDULE IS SHORTENED

Protect the individual exit. In a 55-minute version: 0–7 opening; 7–17 model; 17–30 one investigation; 30–40 drawing; 40–50 exit; 50–55 feedback. Schedule the independent follow-up check next time; do not mark practical performance complete from the abbreviated or supplied-data route.

FORMATIVE CHECKS (how teacher knows what students are getting)

Opening answer: There is observed variation worth checking.

Specific misconception: Different risers immediately identify the builder as the cause

Teacher response: Use consistent finished-surface endpoints and repeat with a checked setup. Compare finish changes and measurement setup before diagnosing.

Exit prompt: Using the five supplied rises, state the spread and a test that separates measurement setup from actual riser variation.

Expected evidence / answer: Spread 1/8 in. Repeat selected risers with consistent endpoints and an independent checked reference; explain the expected result if setup caused the variation.

3 — independent evidence: Spread 1/8 in. Repeat selected risers with consistent endpoints and an independent checked reference; explain the expected result if setup caused the variation. The student explains the method, quantities/units and an appropriate verification or limit without a substantive reasoning cue.

2 — developing evidence: A usable approach is present but one consequential quantity, comparison or explanation is missing, or the student completes it after a reasoning cue. Feedback: Use consistent finished-surface endpoints and repeat with a checked setup. Compare finish changes and measurement setup before diagnosing.

1 — needs instruction: Different risers immediately identify the builder as the cause. The available response does not yet support the target; re-model the comparison and collect new individual evidence.

Rate only the named target from the actual individual evidence. Assess the physics rather than grammar, spelling or use of a scaffold. No evidence / not observed is distinct from an incorrect demonstration. Student self-ratings remain separate.

MATERIALS & READING

Prepare before class: Rule, level, low stair model or approved observation route.

In the application: 1.1 · Every riser in the flight (tu2-s01). Open the same lesson in Present; use its diagram, supplied data, procedure and response prompts.

Print / reference: Unit 2 student materials, pages 2–3. The lesson itself contains the prompts and supplied values if the local packet is unavailable.

Drawing Book assignment: pp. 9-10: sections

If materials or access are unavailable: Use provided readings on paper; mark field measurement not observed.

TEACHER NOTES

Before students arrive: Check zero/reference and the physical setup; prepare one model record, keep the answer key teacher-only, and test the intended class access. Use classroom models or supplied data unless an actual fieldhouse survey has been verified.

Language and access: Keep the diagram visible. Offer 60 seconds of partner rehearsal, the lesson frame and these words: riser, finished surface, vertical, spread, evidence. Accept the supported response modes with unchanged criteria.

Recording in the application: Collect responses in the existing lesson, then use teacher review and the existing 1–2–3 target ratings. Observe actual tool handling separately. Preserve the earlier version when a student revises.

Next teaching decision: Use consistent finished-surface endpoints and repeat with a checked setup. Compare finish changes and measurement setup before diagnosing. Recheck the same idea with a different example before treating it as independently secure.
